clue.text: A water supply at full speed

parts.note: a water main is the large pipe carrying a town's supply

explanation.surface: A water company boasts of its pipes running at full pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning with full force or at top speed, as of a ship driving onward.

clue.text: Adopt a girl-quite young. we hear,

indicators.note: tells the solver the phrase before it is to be spoken, giving a sound rather than spelling

parts.note: a girl is a filly in old slang, and quite young is eight years old, so the phrase is said as 'a filly, eight'

explanation.surface: Someone thinks of adopting a little girl who is still quite young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' says 'a filly, eight' is run together to sound like the answer; filly is old slang for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: To affiliate a child once meant to fix its fatherhood or to take it as one's own, so it is a synonym of adopt.

explanation.surface: Two senses of moving forward together.
explanation.definitionFit: One says 'move along' for go onward, and 'come along with me' for accompany.

clue.text: Cloth "for' girl with a bad knee

parts.note: Nan is a girl's name, short for Ann

indicators.note: a bad knee is out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fabric is bought for a girl who has hurt her knee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges KNEE into KEEN after the name NAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowish cotton fabric first made in Nanking, China, used for trousers.

parts.note: extravagant read as more than is proper in number rather than in spending: men with one wife too many

explanation.surface: Wives complain about husbands who spend too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Men who marry again while still married have an excess of wives, an excess of husbandhood.

clue.text: Frenchman may be torn in pieces.

indicators.note: being torn to pieces leaves the letters scattered, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man from France might be ripped apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Brittany in north-west France is a kind of Frenchman.

parts.note: a household device that records the supply of fuel, and also, playfully, one that measures hot air or idle talk

explanation.surface: A domestic gadget seems to keep track of meaningless chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: Gas is also empty talk, so the household device measures idle words as well as fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic dial counting the fuel piped into a house, gas also meaning idle chatter.

parts.note: the word that sits before crowd in a line of Gray's Elegy and in the title of a Hardy novel

explanation.surface: A gathering of people at a poet and novelist's event.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy has 'Far from the madding crowd's ignoble strife', and Thomas Hardy borrowed it for his novel 'Far from the Madding Crowd'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective, meaning frenzied, that both the poet and the novelist attached to the noun crowd.

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, as the horse sits inside the drink

parts.note: a sling is a spirit-based drink, as in gin sling
a jade is a worn-out horse, also called a hack

explanation.surface: Someone is holding back a tired old horse while drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: A jade is a broken-down horse, as is a hack.
explanation.definitionFit: To shackle is to fetter, so putting someone in chains is a way of holding them back.

explanation.surface: Two materials for a bedroom or a desk.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsheet is part of household linen, and a single leaf of paper is also called this.

explanation.surface: Someone thrashing in water ends up catching flatfish.
explanation.definitionFit: To blunder clumsily through water or mud is one sense; flatfish such as plaice make the other.

parts.note: O is a duck, the cricket score of nought, so Mr O is the male duck

explanation.surface: A man known only by his initial.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a score of nought is a duck because the figure 0 looks like a duck's egg; the male bird of that name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The male of the duck, so the gentleman counterpart of the letter-shaped bird.

parts.note: at the Oval cricket ground, one way a batsman goes out, that is is dismissed

explanation.surface: A notice describes an exit from an oval building.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground; a batsman given out is said to leave, and the leg-before rule is one such way out.
explanation.definitionFit: A mode of dismissal in cricket, when the ball strikes the batsman's leg in front of the stumps.

parts.note: a catch is a kind of part-song sung in canon, so a similar song is meant, not a fielder's catch

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims over a likely catch at a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: The entry reads as two words, a song sung in canon by voices entering in turn, of which a catch is a variety.
explanation.definitionFit: A short canon for voices, of which the catch is a humorous variety.

explanation.surface: Someone forgives faults by failing to notice them.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass over a fault is to forgive it; to fail to notice something is to miss it.

explanation.surface: A thought that may raise the spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship weighing anchor is lifting it up; weighing evidence means considering it.

parts.note: the gravedigger's line in Hamlet, where the missing word names those who tend the soil, the first trade of Adam

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The gravedigger in Hamlet (Act 5) says 'There is no ancient gentlemen but gardeners, ditchers and grave-makers: they hold up Adam's profession.'
explanation.definitionFit: Those who tend gardens, named by the gravedigger as holding the oldest profession, Adam's.

clue.text: A request to turn over the state? "That's' poisonous!

parts.note: PTO, please turn over, is printed at the foot of a page asking the reader to turn it
Maine is a state of the USA

explanation.surface: A petition asks to overthrow the government, which someone calls toxic.
explanation.walkthrough: Turning over the state suggests revolution; it is the page-foot request PTO and the US state of Maine.
explanation.definitionFit: A class of toxic compounds once blamed for food poisoning, so the substance is something poisonous.

clue.text: Henry Vaughan saw it the other night

definitions.text: Henry Vaughan saw it the other night

parts.words: Henry Vaughan saw it the other night
parts.note: the opening line of Vaughan's poem 'The World', where he saw the endless time beyond this life 'like a great ring of pure and endless light'

explanation.surface: A poet reports something he glimpsed recently after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Vaughan's poem 'The World' begins 'I saw Eternity the other night'.
explanation.definitionFit: Endless time, which the seventeenth-century poet claimed to have seen one recent night.

indicators.note: the words come out badly arranged, so the letters of in there are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone peers in and reports that the result is bad news.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of denial, used as 'not either', so it is a negative.

explanation.surface: A dog called Rover works as a keeper in a park.
explanation.definitionFit: A wanderer roams as a rover does; the keeper of a royal park or forest has the same title.

clue.text: A control, it's said, to find fault with

indicators.note: points to a sound, telling the solver the control is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a rein is a strap that controls a horse

explanation.surface: Someone says that a control system is faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' turns 'a rein' into the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To accuse or call to account formally, as a court charges a prisoner, is to censure.

clue.text: Compensate for this process in printing.

explanation.surface: A printer explains how a method makes up for a defect.
explanation.definitionFit: To counterbalance one thing against another; also the printing method transferring ink via a rubber blanket.

clue.text: Colourful victim' of a little velvet-coated gentleman

definitions.text: Colourful victim' of a little velvet-coated gentleman

parts.words: Colourful victim' of a little velvet-coated gentleman
parts.note: a king whose title includes a colour, killed after his horse tripped on a molehill; Jacobites toasted the mole as the little gentleman in black velvet

explanation.surface: A brightly dressed man is attacked by a dapper small gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: King William III (of the House of Orange) died after his horse stumbled on a molehill; Jacobites toasted 'the little gentleman in black velvet', meaning the mole.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch-born king of England whose title names a colour, killed by a fall caused by a mole.

parts.note: the composer whose piano piece Invitation to the Dance was set down in musical notes

explanation.surface: A man's offer of a dance is remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: Carl Maria von Weber wrote the piano rondo 'Invitation to the Dance' (1819); noted means written in musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: The German composer who wrote the piece called Invitation to the Dance.

parts.note: words that name things, rather than verbose objects

explanation.surface: Things with too many words.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar these name a person, place or thing.

explanation.surface: A stallholder speaks in broad terms.
explanation.walkthrough: William Booth founded the Salvation Army and was known as General Booth, so 'generally speaking' is the General giving a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A market stall or kiosk; and William Booth, the General who founded the Salvation Army, is the speaker meant.

explanation.surface: Work begins on a new building for a club.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up or initiate something; also an organisation and its premises, such as a mechanics' hall.

parts.note: the parts of the face that go in front, as the head of a newspaper features page might

explanation.surface: The main articles in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The facial organs that stick out foremost, leading the way.
